title: Machine learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance in respiratory metagenomes
abstract: Background: Targeted therapy for patients with suspected respiratory infections traditionally requires bacterial culture followed by phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), a process that can take up to 5 days. In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), delays in identifying the causative pathogen and its resistance profile may be especially harmful because patients are critically ill and often receive broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics. The growing burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) further complicates clinical decision-making by reducing effective treatment options and increasing the risk of inadequate initial therapy. Culture-free, AI-driven computational metagenomic strategies have the potential to drastically shorten this window, enabling more rapid targeted therapy prescription. To show the feasibility of such approaches, we develop a proof-of-concept framework based on clinical metagenomics. Methods: We simulated respiratory metagenomes using real-world bacterial genomes with associated antimicrobial susceptibility phenotypes. Each simulated metagenome contained a fixed commensal background and one clinically important respiratory pathogen, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, at 5% or 10% bacterial read abundance. Realistic reads were simulated for Oxford Nanopore, PacBio, and Illumina sequencing platforms. Random Forest (RF) classifiers were trained and evaluated using five-fold, strain-grouped cross-validation with fold-specific {chi}2-ranked 13-mer features. ResFinder and KARGA were included as reference-based metagenomics benchmarks and evaluated using the same five held-out folds across the three sequencing platforms and two pathogen-abundance conditions. Results: RF performance varied substantially across species, antibiotics, and sequencing platforms. The strongest and most consistent results were observed for K. pneumoniae, with accuracy reaching approximately 0.96 for ceftazidime, 0.93 for amikacin, and 0.92 for ciprofloxacin. Performance for P. aeruginosa was more heterogeneous: long-read models performed well for amikacin, reaching 0.89 with PacBio and 0.88 with Nanopore, whereas Illumina performed substantially better for ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime, and levofloxacin, reaching accuracies of approximately 0.87, 0.77, and 0.70, respectively. Across most organism-antibiotic combinations, RF accuracy was numerically higher than the classification accuracies obtained with KARGA and ResFinder, which generally remained near 0.50. Increasing pathogen abundance from 5% to 10% and increasing the number of selected features from 2,500 to 5,000 generally produced modest improvements in classification accuracy, although the magnitude of improvement varied across organism-antibiotic combinations and sequencing platforms. Conclusions: Genome-wide k-mer machine learning can recover phenotype-associated antimicrobial resistance signals from simulated respiratory metagenomes, although performance depends strongly on the organism, antibiotic, and sequencing platform. These results represent a simulation-based proof of concept.

title: MAPLE: A hierarchical Multimodal Assistant for Pathology vision-Language Evaluation using logic and reasoning
abstract: Pathological diagnosis requires integration of cellular morphology, tissue architecture, and clinical context across gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs), yet existing vision-language models remain constrained to patch-based analysis with resource-intensive architectures unsuitable for routine clinical deployment. Here we introduce MAPLE, a hierarchical pathology vision-language model that performs whole-slide diagnosis and report generation through efficient multi-scale reasoning. MAPLE employs AgenTile, a small 10-million-parameter vision transformer for cellular-level triage at 40x resolution, achieving segmentation performance equivalent to ~65-fold larger models (e.g., CellViT++) while providing ~95-fold faster inference. Cross-magnification integration with a CLIP-based image encoder at 10x and 5x enables recursive selection of the most diagnostically informative regions per slide. On the PathMMU benchmark (7691 image-question pairs), MAPLE's multimodal (image and text) reasoning module is the first to exceed pathologist performance across all four diagnostic domains (PubMed, EduContent, SocialPath, and Atlas), achieving 70.6-81.2% accuracy versus 68.3-72.9% for pathologists. MAPLE demonstrates calibrated clinical reasoning, appropriately expressing uncertainty for metastatic carcinoma requiring ancillary testing while providing a confident diagnosis for benign hamartoma. These results were validated using an additional clinical cohort. Taken together, our findings establish MAPLE as a computationally efficient, clinically deployable system for AI-augmented pathology, particularly suited to resource-limited settings.

title: Cross-modal RAG: Sub-dimensional Text-to-Image Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Text-to-image generation increasingly demands access to domain-specific, fine-grained, and rapidly evolving knowledge that pretrained models cannot fully capture, necessitating the integration of retrieval methods. Existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods attempt to address this by retrieving globally relevant images, but they fail when no single image contains all desired elements from a complex user query. We propose Cross-modal RAG, a novel framework that decomposes both queries and images into sub-dimensional components, enabling subquery-aware retrieval and generation. Our method introduces a hybrid retrieval strategy, combining a sub-dimensional sparse retriever with a dense retriever, to identify a Pareto-optimal set of images, each contributing complementary aspects of the query. During generation, a multimodal large language model is guided to selectively condition on relevant visual features aligned to specific subqueries for subquery-aware image synthesis. Extensive experiments on MS-COCO, Flickr30K, WikiArt, CUB, and ImageNet-LT demonstrate that Cross-modal RAG significantly outperforms existing baselines in the retrieval and further contributes to generation quality, while maintaining high efficiency.

title: A2Holo: Dual-Stream Flow Matching of 3D Structure and a Protein Language Model for Conformational Transition Prediction
abstract: Modelling a ligand-bound holo conformation from a ligand-free apo conformation is essential in structure-based drug discovery. We present A2Holo, which casts apo-to-holo prediction as flow matching between two experimental structures rather than generation from noise. It transplants the dual-stream joint attention of in-context image generation to residue-aligned protein language model embeddings and structure. Without ligand conditioning or stochastic sampling, A2Holo's single deterministic trajectory reaches a median C RMSD of 0.809 [A] on the D3PM benchmark, the lowest among existing methods. Its TM-score exceeds even the best of 10 samples from every stochastic baseline on at least 144 of 150 pairs. Beyond performance, we directly measure the transplanted multimodal mechanism itself. Because sequence and structure are residue-aligned, its joint attention can be measured at residue resolution and tested for reproducibility across independently trained model variants. Within the structure stream, the attention a residue receives recovers moving residues better than the attention it emits, and this asymmetry is learned. A2Holo demonstrates a successful multimodal transplant from in-context image generation to protein conformational change, with strong deterministic apo-to-holo prediction. It also provides a quantitative account of how that mechanism organises residue-aligned sequence and structure around the residues that move.

title: The unedited acceptance rate: a review-fidelity metric for human-in-the-loop clinical AI
abstract: Objective. Guidance for large language model (LLM) drafting in clinical care relies on human review, yet review is rarely measured as a control. We aimed to define computable measures of review fidelity, establish which a deployed system can compute, and pre-specify their first analysis. Materials and Methods. For a multi-agent clinical system in routine use at one private London outpatient clinic, we defined acceptance coverage, attribution completeness, the unedited acceptance rate (UAR), a bounded normalized edit distance, availability latency and an unedited fast-approval rate (UFA). We checked each measure against the system's code and database structure at a fixed commit on four approval routes and pre-specified a prospective 12-week analysis. Results. The UAR equals the mass at zero of the edit-distance distribution, and availability latency bounds reading time from above only. Clinical documentation keeps draft and signed text with a recorded signer, so the core measures are computable there. Help-desk edit telemetry is written only when the agent's version has been stored. The WhatsApp agent route records no edit signal, and its approver need not be named. No route records when a draft is opened. Documentation accept events were not written before a change committed on November 16, 2026. Model-generated content, including live voice-agent speech, also reaches patients without approval. No measured values are reported. Discussion. Acceptance alone cannot separate accurate drafts from approval without reading, and three of four routes cannot yet support the family. Conclusion. Review fidelity can be specified as telemetry at the approval event. Validation against missed errors is required.

title: MAASAI: A Tool-Augmented Multi-Agent System for Astronomical Data Analysis
abstract: Modern astronomical workflows require the coordinated use of specialised software, scientific archives, heterogeneous data, and domain-specific knowledge. Advances in large language models and multimodal foundation models enable natural-language interaction with scientific data and tools. Realising this potential requires integrating these models with established scientific capabilities. We present MAASAI (Multi-agent Astronomy Assistant for Scientific Analysis and Inference), a modular multi-agent system combining foundation-model reasoning, retrieval-augmented knowledge, and specialised astronomical tools within a graph-based execution framework. MAASAI coordinates request preparation, planning, execution, and response synthesis via specialised workers. Its architecture supports native and external applications, artefact and provenance management, optional human approval, and configurable inference backends, including fully local deployment with open-weight models. Motivated by SKA-era data-analysis challenges, MAASAI is also designed to support other astronomical domains. We evaluate MAASAI through radio-image benchmarks, single- and multi-step workflow demonstrations, and literature-grounded reasoning. Compared with a commercial-model baseline, MAASAI improves macro-averaged F1 scores from 0.53 to 0.72 for extended/diffuse emission classification and from 0.37 to 0.88 for source morphology classification. Workflow demonstrations show the coordination of measurements, source extraction, archive queries, and catalogue processing. A 94-question literature benchmark yielded generally favourable automated assessments, with comparable ratings from a pilot expert evaluation of 59 answers. These results highlight how tool-augmented multi-agent systems extend foundation-model reasoning to specialised astronomical analyses through established scientific software.

title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.

title: Thermodynamically Guided CRISPR Spacer Optimization: Strategy-Dependent Off-Target Trade-Offs.
abstract: Most CRISPR-Cas9 design tools select guide RNAs (gRNAs) by ranking predefined candidates rather than actively optimizing them. Here we instead formulate SpCas9 spacer refinement as a constrained search problem, in which a limited number of nucleotide substitutions may be introduced outside the PAM-proximal seed region. The search is driven by a thermodynamically grounded objective that combines CRISPRspec-based specificity with penalties for suboptimal GC content and long homopolymer runs. Within this single setting we compare five search strategies: three reinforcement-learning (RL) policies, which are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Quantile-Regression Deep Q-Network (QR-DQN), and Rainbow Deep Q-Network (Rainbow DQN), together with a nonlearning score-guided search and a prompt-guided large language model (LLM). All five share the same objective, mutable positions, substitution budget, and evaluation protocol, so that only the search strategy differs. On 100 held-out IGF2R guides from a gene and chromosome excluded from training, every strategy significantly reduced the predicted off-target burden (38.6-78.3%) and improved independent specificity metrics without degrading on-target scores. The strategies nevertheless differed sharply in per-guide safety: the LLM achieved the largest aggregate reduction but introduced new off-target sites into 38% of guides that were initially free of them, whereas PPO, an on-policy RL algorithm, retained a strong gain with the lowest regression rate of 15%. These results show that the thermodynamic objective supplies a robust common optimization signal, while the choice of search strategy governs the trade-off between aggregate improvement and regression of already-favorable guides.

title: HealthFound: a health world model for quantitative reasoning on longitudinal health profiles
abstract: Medical large language models have shown promise in medical knowledge retrieval and clinical reasoning but remain limited in quantitative reasoning over longitudinal health data, partly due to the lack of effective data construction and model training strategies tailored to large-scale prospective cohorts. Here, we present HealthFound, a health world model trained on 12.4 million constructed examples, including 14-year longitudinal biomedical records from 501,936 participants and datasets for medical knowledge and general reasoning. We propose a three-stage training framework comprising progressive curriculum supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled retention fine-tuning, and task-verifiable policy optimization. This enables the model to effectively parse heterogeneous quantitative data and perform robust quantitative reasoning about incident diseases and health trajectories. HealthFound achieves the highest mean accuracy across eight public medical benchmarks. On the task of predicting 1,074 future disease onsets, it outperforms the closest large language model by approximately 10 percentage points on average. In two independent external validations (MIMIC-IV and NHANES), it demonstrates superior zero-shot generalization, achieving improvements of over 5.2% across 417 disease endpoints. The model also achieves top results on tasks involving literature-derived question answering and quantitative indicator imputation. Furthermore, HealthFound generates interpretable reasoning rationales that are consistent with established biomedical knowledge. Collectively, our results demonstrate that HealthFound enables medical LLMs to evolve from static knowledge repositories into dynamic quantitative reasoning engines over longitudinal health data.

title: Contextualizing Biological Language Models across Modalities via Logit-Space Contrastive Alignment
abstract: Pretrained biological language models encode rich probabilistic structure through native token distributions, but multimodal adaptation typically aligns hidden representations or replaces the native likelihood interface with task-specific heads. We introduce LOGICA (Logit-space Contrastive Alignment), whose central methodological change is to align the context-conditioned native token distributions themselves rather than pooled latent representations. Using native-head-preserving cross-modal adapters, LOGICA couples models with distinct vocabularies and tokenization schemes without requiring a shared tokenizer, decoder, or embedding space. Contrastive learning operates directly through each model's original token-likelihood interface, enabling mutation-local ranking, cross-modal dependency mapping, and context-guided sequence design without task-specific heads. Across protein-ligand, TCR-peptide, and drug-resistance tasks, LOGICA outperforms matched latent-contrastive and conditional-MLM baselines, particularly in low-homology, mutation-local, and data-scarce regimes. These results support native-logit alignment as a general strategy for making pretrained biological token distributions context-sensitive without sacrificing their probabilistic semantics.

title: RumiFold: Teaching an LLM to Natively Fold Proteins and Reason About Their Function
abstract: Can we teach a general-purpose language model to fold proteins? And if so, what does learning to fold enable beyond structure prediction itself? We introduce RumiFold, a pretrained chat model that learns to predict protein structures directly from its own hidden states. RumiFold processes proteins through repeated folding passes, then uses these folded representations to answer questions in natural language. It achieves folding accuracy comparable to dedicated single-representation models such as SimpleFold, alongside state-of-the-art performance on Gene Ontology protein function prediction and free-text function description. We find that folding pretraining organizes the model's hidden states around protein function, creating an internal per-residue workspace that is biologically grounded. Causal interventions show that this folded workspace links structure and language when RumiFold predicts function, providing rich representations for biomolecular reasoning. We see RumiFold as a step toward native biomolecular intelligence: where protein-based computations and language-based reasoning become integrated capabilities of general-purpose language models. Code, data, and models are available at: https://rumifold.baulab.info

title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.

title: Deciphering state bridges via a single-cell large language model
abstract: Large-scale single-cell transcriptomic data provide a new avenue for precision medicine by uncovering cellular heterogeneity. However, systematic comparison of remodeling patterns across various biological states remains unavailable. Here, we first developed a computational framework based on a foundation model of single cell biology, Universal Cell Embedding (UCE), to harmonize annotations comprising 36 cell types. Based on an integrated dataset of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with 8,789 human samples comprising more than 59 million cells or nuclei across 614 biological states, we then embedded each state with a 36-dimensional vector in a unified space of cell-composition change and further deciphered states bridges by analyzing the relationships among the 614 state vectors. As a result, 22,161 significant bridges (P < 0.05) between the 614 states were revealed. Moreover, we successfully identified a number of well-known bridges such as bridge between Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease (P = 2.21e-15), suggesting the effectiveness of the proposed framework. More importantly, we uncovered a number of new bridges. Furthermore, analyses of the number of changed cell types (NCC) and Shannon entropy revealed heterogeneous and tissue-dependent patterns of cellular composition remodeling. This study provides a new strategy for identifying disease associations and potential therapeutic relationships by deciphering bridges between biological states from scRNA-seq landscape.

title: LLM-Based Assistant for Dog Care Guidance
abstract: This study investigates whether domain grounding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) can enhance the accuracy and reliability of pet care advice generated by large language models (LLMs). We curated a dataset of breed-specific dog care information and used it to develop two systems: a RAG pipeline based on TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B model adapted using LoRA. Both systems were evaluated on 15 dog care questions. The RAG model achieved a perfect average score of 2.0, outperforming the fine-tuned model (mean = 1.47). Statistical analyses, including Welch's t-test, Mann-Whitney U, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (all p < 0.05), confirmed the significance of the performance gap. Our findings suggest that retrieval-based domain grounding leads to more accurate, consistent, and trustworthy responses than standalone fine-tuning in specialized LLM applications.

title: Genome-to-Image Translation: Reconstructing Escherichia coli Morphology from Genomic Sequences
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is established in routine practice by culture-based susceptibility testing, which is slow relative to the clinical need for an early treatment decision. Resistance status also leaves a measurable trace in cell morphology, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates is increasingly available, which raises the question of whether colony appearance can be predicted directly from an isolate's genome. We formulate this as a conditional image-generation problem. The assembled contigs of each isolate are encoded into a single 768-dimensional vector by a frozen genomic language model through a segment-contig-isolate aggregation hierarchy, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance label. We train on 167,356 single-cell images from 22 clinical blood isolates imaged under azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and a no-drug control, compare seven pretrained convolutional backbones inside the generator, and select ConvNeXt-Tiny on distributional image-quality metrics. The synthetic images are then assessed extrinsically: added to a reduced real training set, they improve per-antibiotic resistance classification, with a significant gain in resistant-class recall.

title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data or generated outputs. We evaluated selected functionalities of a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, restricted here to unconditional protein-backbone generation, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools may have been included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-weight coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability on some tasks, though no clear reproduction of the most complex tool we evaluate. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers may need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of selected functionalities, based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or weaken dual-use managed access strategies.

title: DeepQuest: From Knowledge Gaps to Scientific Discovery in Alzheimer's Disease
abstract: Automating experiments does not necessarily advance scientific understanding. Research agents must identify meaningful knowledge gaps, determine what available data can resolve, and assess whether their findings advance existing knowledge. We introduce DeepQuest, a knowledge-gap-driven AI scientist framework for Alzheimer's disease research. DeepQuest transforms unresolved questions from domain reviews into traceable, testable hypotheses and prioritizes them through data feasibility screening and groupwise Elo ranking. It couples iterative experimentation with two-level auditing that separates experimental reliability from knowledge contribution relative to two frozen literature corpora. On OASIS-3, DeepQuest produces 42 feasible hypotheses and outperforms the strongest baselines in 14 of 15 evaluator-dimension comparisons across three language-model reviewers. The full framework achieves an audit-assessed scientific finding rate of 95.24%, outperforming both general-purpose executors and domain-specific research agents. This scientific finding rate remains stable across literature corpora and evaluator model families. Representative findings concern neuropsychiatric symptoms and dementia risk, longitudinal amyloid spatial stability, and neocortical tau-associated clinical impairment, with key associations supported in independent ADNI and AIBL cohorts. These results show how aligning knowledge gaps, data feasibility, and evidence auditing can turn automated research into traceable, evidence-supported scientific discovery. Our source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DeepQuest-3066/

title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.

title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Relation Extraction within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework
abstract: Information Extraction (IE) plays a pivotal role in transforming unstructured data into structured formats, such as Knowledge Graphs. One of the main tasks within IE is Relation Extraction (RE), which identifies relations between entities in text data. This process enriches the semantic understanding of documents, enabling more precise information retrieval and query answering. Recent works leveraging pre-trained language models have demonstrated significant performance improvements in RE. In the current era of Large Language Models (LLMs), fine-tuning these LLMs can mitigate the limitations of zero-shot RE methods, particularly in overcoming the domain adaptation challenges inherent in RE. This work explores not only the effectiveness of fine-tuned LLMs but also their integration into a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based RE approach to address domain adaptation challenges when general-purpose LLMs serve as generators within the RAG framework. Empirical evaluations on the TACRED, TACRED-Revisited (TACREV), and Re-TACRED datasets reveal substantial performance improvements with fine-tuned LLMs, such as Llama2-7B, Mistral-7B, and Flan-T5 Large and surpass previous methods on these datasets.

title: SHAKTI: Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI for Nutrition and Health
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) answer many diet and health questions but can state unsupported claims and cite sources that do not support them. We present SHAKTI (Smart Health Advisor for Knowledge-based Tailored Interventions), a conversational assistant that answers only from retrieved scholarly papers and exact food-composition data, and evaluate it with retrieval, generation, grounding, efficiency and contextawareness metrics. We indexed 484,368,086 OpenAlex works, searched exactly on a GPU for evaluation (10,065 NFCorpus, BioASQ, SciFact and PubMedQA questions) and through a compressed 230-million-abstract index in deployment. On 1,000 stratified questions, we compared single-shot, multi-hop, corrective and deep-research retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with Claude Sonnet. SHAKTI adds conversational query rewriting, USDA FoodData Central lookups, source-link checks and online verification of quotes and numbers. It was tested in 36 scripted conversational turns, a 248-question memory-depth test and a 38-question load test. Claims were checked by a Claude Opus judge against exactly the text the system saw. MedCPT reranking of hybrid retrieval gave the best MRR (0.21) and MAP@100 (0.14). Across existing RAG methods, faithfulness was 0.95-0.96, claim hallucination 0.5-0.8% and context precision up to 0.98; the deep-research agent answered 73.2% of BioASQ questions correctly. In conversation, SHAKTI reached a context-awareness score of 97.1%, faithfulness 95.5%, 1.9% unsupported claims, no contradicted claims and 229/229 working source links; it resolved references to the first question after 16 unrelated questions. An answer cost 14,716 tokens (US$0.06) with a median latency of 24 s. Large-scale retrieval with agentic evidence selection and mechanical verification yields auditable, low-hallucination nutrition answers.

title: Segment Anything In-Context via Visual Demonstrations
abstract: We present the Segment Anything Model via Visual Demonstrations (SAYD), a foundation model for in-context segmentation. Given visual demos comprising prompt images and their segmentation masks, SAYD segments coherent regions (e.g., objects or their parts) in a query image by establishing visual correspondences between the prompts and the query. SAYD generalizes to previously-unseen segmentation tasks, including those requiring tacit visual knowledge or involving concepts that are difficult to articulate unambiguously in language. We train SAYD on 12 public datasets originally curated for panoptic segmentation using our proposed techniques, including a lightweight mask decoder for prompt-agnostic mask generation and a learning mechanism for recognizing novel query classes absent in the prompts. These innovations enhance both computational efficiency and out-of-domain generalization. Consequently, SAYD significantly outperforms existing methods of in-context segmentation and open-vocabulary segmentation across 24 out-of-domain benchmarks, spanning natural, biological, ecological, cosmological, medical, pathological, and satellite imagery.

title: Enabling Validation for Robust Few-Shot Recognition
abstract: A key challenge in Few-Shot Recognition (FSR) is the scarcity of labeled task-specific data for training. Contemporary methods mitigate this challenge by exploiting pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for their learned transferable features. Some recent ones augment the scarce data by retrieving relevant yet out-of-distribution (OOD) examples from external data sources. However, they largely overlook an equally fundamental challenge: the absence of validation data for model selection and hyperparameter tuning. As a result, the adapted VLMs overfit the few-shot training data and generalize poorly to OOD test data. We show that retrieved data provide a natural source of validation, but their direct use creates a fundamental paradox. Since the retrieved samples are inherently OOD w.r.t the few-shot ID training data, adapting a VLM to the ID data constantly degrades its performance on the retrieved data. Consequently, conventional validation relying on the accuracy of retrieved data favors no adaptation and prevents improved generalization. To resolve this dilemma, we formulate validation as a multi-objective optimization (MOO) problem between performance gains on the few-shot ID data and the performance preservation on the retrieved data. We introduce a simple yet effective validation strategy by choosing an operating point on the Pareto front of the MOO problem. This strategy enables hyperparameter tuning, which had been unrealistically done by using test data, thereby mitigating overfitting and improving generalization. We integrate it into a stage-wise finetuning pipeline, termed Validation-Enabled Stage-wise Tuning (VEST). Extensive experiments on five established benchmarks show that VEST consistently outperforms existing approaches on both ID and OOD test data.

title: Graph-based Nearest Neighbors with Dynamic Updates via Random Walks
abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANN) is a common way to retrieve relevant search results, especially now in the context of large language models and retrieval augmented generation. One of the most widely used algorithms for ANN is based on constructing a multi-layer graph over the dataset, called the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). While this algorithm supports insertion of new data, it does not support deletion of existing data. Moreover, deletion algorithms described by prior work come at the cost of increased query latency, decreased recall, or prolonged deletion time. In this paper, we propose a new theoretical framework for graph-based ANN based on random walks. We then utilize this framework to analyze a randomized deletion approach that approximately preserves hitting time statistics compared to the graph before deleting the point. However, this guarantee needs at least as many edge samples as there are edges in the clique over the neighbors of the deleted point. We then turn this theoretical framework into a deterministic deletion algorithm, and show that it provides a better tradeoff between query latency, recall, deletion time, and memory usage through an extensive collection of experiments.

title: BMAM: Brain-inspired Multi-Agent Memory Framework
abstract: Language-model-based agents operating over extended interaction horizons face persistent challenges in preserving temporally grounded information and maintaining behavioral consistency across sessions, a failure mode we term soul erosion. We present BMAM (Brain-inspired Multi-Agent Memory), a general-purpose memory architecture that models agent memory as a set of functionally specialized subsystems rather than a single unstructured store. Inspired by cognitive memory systems, BMAM decomposes memory into episodic, semantic, salience-aware, and control-oriented components that operate at complementary time scales, organised as a six-phase memory lifecycle. To support long-horizon reasoning, BMAM organises episodic memories along explicit timelines and retrieves evidence by fusing multiple complementary signals. Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark show that BMAM achieves 78.45% accuracy, outperforming seven memory-augmented baselines. Pairwise ablations reveal super-additive synergy between brain-region components rather than redundant stacking, and a Soul Portability Test demonstrates 87.5% identity-integrity across full memory export, clear, and restore. A targeted refinement of the temporal-trigger heuristics raises LongMemEval multi-session accuracy from 45.2% to 56.4%, validating the architectural decomposition behind BMAM. Code is available at https://github.com/innovation64/BMAM.

title: Unleashing the Value of Raw Point Clouds for 3D Understanding with LLMs
abstract: Standard 3D point cloud language models typically rely on pretrained point encoders to extract 3D features and project them into representations processable by large language models (LLMs). However, these encoders are often originally optimized for pre-defined tasks, resulting in a representation bottleneck that may lead to a substantial mismatch with downstream 3D understanding. Moreover, existing models largely follow a single pass closed-book generation, limiting their ability to actively inspect task-relevant 3D regions or retrieve necessary external knowledge. In this work, we present PointTool, an encoder-free and tool-augmented framework for 3D reasoning. PointTool introduces Alignment-Free Patch Tokenization (AFPT) to locally aggregate raw point clouds while preserving fine-grained geometric structure, and Decoupled Point-Text LoRA (DPL) to facilitate global aggregation and 3D knowledge internalization within a frozen LLM. Building upon these designs, Program-Supervised Tool Reasoning (PSTR) enables the model to explicitly operate on raw 3D data and external resources through executable tools, supporting interactive 3D reasoning grounded in spatial evidence. We further introduce PointCloud-TR, a benchmark comprising 13K 3D objects, 39.8K questions, and 35.6K tool trajectories to facilitate training and evaluation of complex 3D reasoning. Experiments demonstrate that PointTool achieves strong performance on both standard and complex 3D understanding tasks, validating the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title: Enhancing Code Consistency in AI Research with Large Language Models and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Ensuring that code accurately reflects the algorithms and methods described in research papers is critical for maintaining credibility and fostering trust in AI research. This paper presents a novel system designed to verify code implementations against the algorithms and methodologies outlined in corresponding research papers. Our system employs Retrieval-Augmented Generation to extract relevant details from both the research papers and code bases, followed by a structured comparison using Large Language Models. This approach improves the accuracy and comprehensiveness of code implementation verification while contributing to the transparency, explainability, and reproducibility of AI research. By automating the verification process, our system reduces manual effort, enhances research credibility, and ultimately advances the state of the art in code verification.

title: SGR3 Model: Scene Graph Retrieval-Reasoning Model in 3D
abstract: 3D scene graphs provide a structured representation of object entities and their relationships, enabling high-level interpretation and reasoning for robots while remaining intuitively understandable to humans. Existing approaches for 3D scene graph generation typically combine scene reconstruction with graph neural networks (GNNs). However, such pipelines require multi-modal data that may not always be available, and their reliance on heuristic graph construction can constrain the prediction of relationship triplets. In this work, we introduce a Scene Graph Retrieval-Reasoning Model in 3D (SGR3 Model), a training-free framework that leverages multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for semantic scene graph generation. SGR3 Model bypasses the need for explicit 3D reconstruction. Instead, it enhances relational reasoning by incorporating semantically aligned scene graphs retrieved via a ColPali-style cross-modal framework. To improve retrieval robustness, we further introduce a weighted patch-level similarity selection mechanism that mitigates the negative impact of blurry or semantically uninformative regions. Experiments demonstrate that SGR3 Model achieves competitive performance compared to training-free baselines and on par with GNN-based expert models. Moreover, an ablation study on the retrieval module and knowledge base scale reveals that retrieved external information is explicitly integrated into the token generation process, rather than being implicitly internalized through abstraction.

title: CogRAG: Tackling Heterogeneous Cognitive Demands in RAG via Stratified Retrieval and Reasoning
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks typically process all queries through a one-size-fits-all pipeline, ignoring the heterogeneous cognitive demands of different tasks. This cognitive-blind approach causes two failure modes: cascading errors when low-level factual gaps trigger hallucinated reasoning, and reasoning-answer inconsistency in higher-order analytical tasks. We introduce CogRAG, a training-free, domain-agnostic framework that tackles these heterogeneous cognitive demands via stratified retrieval and reasoning. Inspired by Bloom's Taxonomy, CogRAG uses the predicted cognitive load of a query as a central control signal that coordinates two modules: Cognition-Adaptive Evidence Refinement supplements missing context via fact-centric or option-centric paths, and Cognition-Stratified Structured Reasoning replaces unconstrained chain-of-thought with cognition-aligned reasoning templates. We evaluate CogRAG on a demanding professional testbed, the Registered Dietitian qualification examination. CogRAG effectively reduces early-stage factual errors and eliminates reasoning-answer inconsistency, raising Qwen3-8B accuracy from 73.4\% to 85.8\% in single-choice mode and from 63.3\% to 80.5\% in scenario mode. These results highlight cognitive-stratified control as an effective, generalizable paradigm for reliable complex reasoning in large language models.

title: Structure-Exploiting Hierarchical Retrieval for Long Narrative Documents: A Precision-Oriented Alternative to Learned Abstraction Trees
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over book-length documents must locate a small, coherent set of passages inside tens of thousands of tokens. Flat dense retrieval ignores document structure; RAPTOR instead builds a hierarchy by recursively clustering and summarizing with a language model. We study a complementary design that exploits the native structure of a document: a two-level retriever that (i) selects chapters with a hybrid BM25+dense match over chapter recaps, (ii) runs a chapter-filtered dense search, and (iii) expands top passages into contiguous, section-aware spans under a token budget, plus content-hash-gated delta ingestion to keep the index cheap to update. We evaluate on five public-domain books (113 chapter-localization queries) and on QuALITY and NovelQA (200K+ token novels). In-house, we find a seed-stable precision/ranking tradeoff: with section expansion off, hierarchical retrieval returns a higher fraction of chunks from the correct chapter (+3.3pp, Wilcoxon p=0.014); with expansion on, ranking improves (MRR, p=0.040). Accuracy differences are not significant. On QuALITY, hierarchical retrieval beats flat top-k (81.0% vs 70.4%, p=0.0019) and matches the full article (p=0.74). On NovelQA, hierarchical and flat retrieval are statistically tied (55.7% vs 56.8%, p=0.24); hierarchy helps aggregation questions while flat wins on localized facts. Against a faithful RAPTOR baseline we find a complementary tradeoff, not superiority. Delta ingestion reuses 94 to 99.7% of embeddings on incremental edits. We make no claim of semantic chapter-boundary inference and scope claims to English narrative prose.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Agentic Era: Tradition, Present, and Prospect
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) couples frozen language models with external, updatable knowledge, so that generation is grounded in retrieved evidence rather than in parametric memory alone. This work maps RAG in the agentic era by joining them on a single lifecycle axis, from offline indexing through pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and orchestration over these stages. It treats indexing and orchestration as first-class components and agentic workflows as a paradigm of their own, and it covers the agentic work that has appeared since those reviews. Beyond these components, it covers evaluation, applications, and the questions that remain open for future exploration. From tradition to present and beyond, this work systematically reviews RAG from a perspective of the agentic era.

title: MusicRec: Audio, Lyrics, and Engagement Feature Enrichment for Music Recommendation
abstract: Music recommendation systems typically treat songs as opaque tokens, relying on interaction histories that overlook semantic or acoustic content. Prior LLM-augmented, multimodal, and text-enhanced sequential recommenders partially combine semantic, acoustic, or engagement signals, and none jointly model all three within a unified LLM-based framework grounded in song content. In this work, we propose a multimodal framework for session-based music recommendation that enriches the LastFM-1K dataset with three complementary signals: (1) audio and lyric embeddings from pretrained music and text models, (2) LLM-generated semantic metadata using the MGPHot schema, and (3) listening completion ratios. We validate the generated metadata against human MGPHot annotations across all 58 attributes. We extend the E4SRec framework with multimodal features, ItemID encoder backbones including SASRec, BERT4Rec, and GRU4Rec, and LLM backbones including LLaMA-2-13B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and LLaMA-3-70B across zero-shot and fine-tuned settings. In addition, we evaluate four multimodal fusion strategies, benchmark five audio and five lyric encoders, and compare Spotify audio attributes with LLM-generated MGPHot metadata. Our experiments show that content-based features improve over ID-only baselines by up to 95% in Recall and 79% in NDCG, with the largest gains when the ItemID baseline is weakest. Fine-tuning substantially improves over zero-shot, after which the best audio or lyric setup outperforms the ID-only baseline for every backbone. Naive multimodal fusion does not always yield additive improvements, highlighting challenges in cross-modal integration, while structured LLM-generated metadata proves more useful than Spotify audio attributes. We release a large-scale multimodal benchmark for music recommendation research.

title: ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs for Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing
abstract: Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.

title: GENECraft: A Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System for Controllable Regulatory DNA Design
abstract: Designing regulatory DNA requires reconciling two complementary modeling paradigms: genomic language models (gLMs) capture evolutionary syntax without guaranteeing targeted regulatory activity, whereas sequence-to-function predictors provide explicit functional supervision without enforcing native-like sequence plausibility. We introduce GENECraft, a training-free Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System (FP-DDS) that couples a genomic language model (Carbon) and a functional oracle (AlphaGenome) during inference-time optimization to balance predicted regulatory activity and consistency with genomic sequence priors. GENECraft evolves continuous latent nucleotide logits while evaluating strictly decoded discrete DNA sequences under a time-dependent composite vector field that fuses normalized functional utility, bidirectional contextual prior guidance, and compositional quality penalties, followed by feasibility-first trajectory readout. Across 2,185 loci spanning promoters, multi-constraint enhancers, and 18 transcription factors (TFs), GENECraft achieves full-joint success rates of 62.70%, 65.23%, and 94.56% (macro-averaged), substantially outperforming seven optimization, evolutionary, and generative baselines (which reach at most 2.15% on enhancers). In matched 336-locus ablations, in-loop Carbon guidance reduces native-relative dinucleotide divergence by 7.8--11.5%, enhancer context sensitivity by 10.5%, and TF mutation sensitivity by 11.0%, establishing FP-DDS as a principled framework for controllable regulatory DNA design.

title: From Technical Performance to Clinical Impact: Challenges and Opportunities for AI Modelling of CKD Progression.
abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major global health burden, with highly heterogeneous trajectories ranging from long-term stability to rapid progression towards kidney failure and kidney replacement therapy. Accurate prediction of CKD progression is essential to support personalised monitoring, timely therapeutic intensification, nephrology referral, and preparation for advanced kidney care. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) approaches may improve risk stratification by modelling complex, nonlinear, and time-dependent patterns in routinely collected clinical data, electronic health records, and potentially multimodal data sources. Nonetheless, it remains unclear how ready these AI-driven models are for clinical use. This structured narrative review aimed to map the current landscape of AI for predicting CKD progression, assess the robustness and clinical relevance of the evidence, and identify methodological and implementation gaps that must be addressed to translate technical accuracy into clinical impact. This review synthesised 35 studies published between 2020 and 2025 that developed and evaluated models to predict CKD progression. Most studies used retrospective cohort designs and electronic health record data, relying mainly on demographic variables, laboratory measures, comorbidities, and clinical history. Tree-based models, random forests, boosting methods, regression-based approaches, and neural networks were the most commonly investigated methods. Overall, the reviewed models often achieved favourable discriminative performance, as measured by AUROC or C-index. Nevertheless, the evidence base remains limited by substantial heterogeneity in study designs, cohort compositions, prediction targets, time horizons, feature engineering, and validation strategies. External validation was reported in only about one-quarter of studies, while calibration, clinical utility, patient-level uncertainty, and implementation-oriented evaluation were inconsistently addressed. Prediction endpoints were predominantly kidney failure-related. Multimodal data, including imaging, genomics, and social determinants of health, were rarely used, and explainability methods were more often applied for model description than for clinician-facing decision support. AI models show substantial promise for predicting CKD progression, particularly when trained on routinely available clinical data. However, the field remains more advanced in model development than in clinical validation and implementation. Future research should prioritise external and temporal validation, systematic calibration assessment, decision-curve or net-benefit analysis, comparison with established clinical risk scores, clinically meaningful prediction horizons, subgroup and fairness evaluation, patient-level uncertainty estimation, and prospective testing of model-informed care. These steps are essential to move from statistically accurate models to reliable, interpretable, equitable, and actionable tools for CKD management.

title: The Therapeutic Pipeline: Future Treatments and Precision Medicine.
abstract: Rare interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) represent a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by various pathogenic mechanisms, clinical presentations, prognoses, and therapeutic challenges. Among these, acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD), pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PLCH) exemplify rare pulmonary diseases driven by distinct biological mechanisms, including lysosomal dysfunction, impaired surfactant homeostasis, and activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK) pathways. Recent advancements in molecular biology, genomics, and translational research boosted the development of precision medicine strategies and disease-specific therapies for these conditions. This narrative review was conducted in accordance with the SANRA guidelines. A thorough literature search of the PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus databases was performed from January 2000 to June 2026. Significant progress has been made in treating all three diseases. In ASMD, enzyme replacement therapy with olipudase alfa has greatly improved visceral and lung symptoms, while research in gene therapy, gene editing, and metabolic treatments is ongoing. For PAP, inhaled granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) is now the primary disease-specific treatment, now supported by phase III trial evidence for inhaled molgramostim, complemented by potential therapies such as immunomodulation, macrophage transplantation, and gene-based strategies. In PLCH, the discovery of recurrent MAPK pathway variants has supported the use of genotype-targeted treatments with B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine (BRAF)/threonine kinase and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) kinase inhibitors. Under these conditions, advances in molecular diagnostics, circulating biomarkers, quantitative high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT), radiomics, and artificial intelligence (AI) are poised to enhance diagnosis, patient stratification, prognosis, and treatment decisions. ASMD, PAP, and PLCH are entering into an era of precision medicine, in which disease-specific molecular mechanisms play an increasing role in guiding diagnosis and treatment. Ongoing integration of genomics, biomarkers, advanced imaging, AI, and targeted therapies could revolutionize the management of conditions such as ASMD, PAP, and PLCH, leading to better long-term patient outcomes.

title: CRC tumor antigens and immune escape: Designing peptide vaccines for colorectal Cancer.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of global cancer mortality, with current therapies often limited by toxicity and resistance. Immunotherapy, particularly peptide-based vaccines, represents a promising alternative by eliciting targeted immune responses. This review provides a critical and comparative synthesis of CRC peptide vaccine development, distinguishing itself from previous reviews by integrating mechanistic insights into immune evasion with a structured framework that connects antigen selection, epitope identification (experimental and computational), and clinical translation. We specifically highlight two underexplored areas: tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs) and the critical distinction between microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) and microsatellite stable (MSS) CRC, which fundamentally dictates mutational burden, neoantigen load, and vaccine responsiveness. We first detail the sophisticated mechanisms of immune evasion employed by CRC, including an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment enriched with regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs), dysregulated antigen presentation via HLA class I alterations, and expression of inhibitory checkpoints. The review critically evaluates methods for epitope identification, contrasting traditional experimental approaches with modern computational strategies that leverage genomics, AI, and immunoinformatics tools for predicting high-affinity, immunogenic epitopes. We emphasize that predicted immunogenicity does not equate to clinical efficacy, and we critically appraise the limitations of current computational tools, including high false-positive rates and poor correlation with in vivo immunogenicity. While promising, challenges remain, including low immunogenicity, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) restriction, and tumor heterogeneity. Future success likely depends on developing multi-epitope, personalized vaccines combined with adjuvants and immune checkpoint inhibitors to enhance efficacy. In conclusion, peptide vaccines offer a precise and adaptable platform for CRC immunotherapy, holding significant potential for improving clinical outcomes through targeted immune activation.

title: From Head to Tail: LLM-Augmented Sequential Recommendation and Trade-off Optimization
abstract: Recommender systems exhibit popularity bias, often under-serving long-tail and cold-start items with sparse interaction data. We propose a group-specific data augmentation approach that leverages LLMs to generate synthetic interactions, formulated as a constrained optimization problem, maximizing group-specific NDCG@20 and coverage while bounding overall NDCG@20 degradation within an acceptable threshold. Items are partitioned by interaction frequency to find the optimal augmentation strategy for each group. We further study combining the augmentation across groups simultaneously and find that while individual optimal strategies navigate the multi-group augmentation design, they are not simply additive. We further ablate on the LLM-based augmentation itself, comparing LLM scales, augmentation configuration under token constraints, finding that augmentation quality scales with contextual richness, albeit at a proportionally higher cost. Experiments with SASRec demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving over 100% and 60% improvement in group-specific NDCG@20 for extreme and regular long-tail items, respectively, on our industrial dataset, and 40%, 25% for MovieLens-32M, while increasing their coverage without significant overall degradation.

title: From Clever Hans to Hypotheses: Interpreting EEG Foundational Transformers with LRP
abstract: Emerging foundation models (FMs) in electroencephalography (EEG) promise a path to scale deep learning in diagnostics and brain-computer interfaces despite data scarcity, yet their opaque nature remains a barrier to wider adoption. We investigate attention-aware Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) as a post-hoc attribution method for EEG-FMs, extending LRP's use on convolutional neural network (CNN)-based EEG models to the Transformer architectures that current FMs are based on. We find that LRP can both verify EEG-FM decisions and surface novel, biologically plausible hypotheses from them. In motor imagery, it unmasks 'Clever Hans' behavior where models prioritize task correlated ocular signals over the intended motor correlates. In a naturalistic paradigm for affect prediction, it reveals a recurring reliance on a central electrode cluster, suggesting a candidate sensorimotor signature of arousal. Though heatmap interpretation remains ambiguous in this complex domain, the results position LRP as a tool for both verification and exploration of EEG-FMs, a role that will grow in both importance and discovery potential as the underlying models mature.

title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.

title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Persian Legal Question Answering
abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.

title: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration
abstract: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs. Our code is available at https://github.com/tianyi-lab/EpiCompass.

title: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever
abstract: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.

title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring
abstract: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.

title: MH-RAG-DIVE: Dynamic and Cost-Efficient Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via Tree-Cached Dialogue Simulation
abstract: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. We introduce MH-RAG-DIVE, a dynamic interactive user simulation framework designed to evaluate RAG systems in more complex multi-hop and multi-turn settings. The framework extends RAG-DIVE with a Context Discoverer, which identifies documents that can be combined to generate multi-hop questions within an ongoing conversation. To address the high computational cost of dynamic user simulation, we further introduce a Conversation Cacher, which reuses turns from previous evaluation runs while preserving the dynamic nature of the evaluation. We evaluate the framework across six distinct RAG configurations and compare its results with the original RAG-DIVE evaluation and the static, human-created CLAPNQ dataset. Our experiments show consistent performance trends across the evaluation approaches, while the more complex multi-hop and multi-turn setting exposes additional challenges for RAG systems. Furthermore, the Conversation Cacher substantially reduces token consumption, demonstrating its potential to make dynamic evaluation more cost-efficient. Finally, we apply MH-RAG-DIVE to an industrial RAG system with domain-specific data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world evaluation scenarios. Overall, our results show that the proposed approach provides a more complex and cost-efficient framework for evaluating RAG systems. All code and experimental data are publicly available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Daniel-Innsbruck/MH-RAG-DIVE).

title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance
abstract: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.

title: MemChain: Learning Interpretable Memory Traces for Memory-Augmented LLM Agents
abstract: Memory-augmented LLM agents typically answer queries by retrieving relevant memories and feeding them directly to an answer model. This retrieval-as-evidence paradigm assumes retrieved memories are already suitable for reasoning, leaving the answer model to resolve redundancy, conflicts, and weak relevance while incurring substantial context overhead in long-term memory tasks. We propose MemChain, a trainable post-retrieval memory policy that transforms retrieved candidates into answer-facing active memory, represented as a compact and grounded evidence context. Given a user query and retrieved candidates, MemChain first generates a question-conditioned evidence plan, then constructs an ordered grounded evidence trace that organizes retrieved memories according to their semantic roles and dependencies, and finally executes explicit memory actions to produce a concise evidence context for answer generation. To train the mediator, we introduce a two-stage learning framework. Supervised trace learning first teaches the policy to generate structurally valid plans, traces, actions, and evidence contexts. We then propose Trace-Guided Memory Policy Optimization (TMPO), a reinforcement learning objective that optimizes the memory policy using downstream answer quality while jointly encouraging trace grounding, evidence support, structural validity, and answer stability across multiple rollouts. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S demonstrate that MemChain consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across both closed-source and open-weight frozen answer models while substantially reducing the memory context passed to the answer model.

title: RAVEN: A Self-RAG Based Agent for Threat Classification and Response
abstract: Security event analysis in large enterprises can be overwhelming, as each alert typically requires manual in- spection by human operators. This process is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies, especially in high-volume Secu- rity Operations Center (SOC) environments. In this work- in-progress paper, we present RAVEN: Retrieval-Augmented Vulnerability & Event aNalysis, an agentic framework designed to support SOC analysts by automating the initial stages of alert investigation. The proposed system leverages a Self- Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based approach to provide an initial classification of security events and enables interactive refinement through analyst-in-the-loop queries. Un- like traditional approaches that rely on generic mitigation strategies, RAVEN generates context-aware remediation sug- gestions by incorporating knowledge of the target enterprise infrastructure. We implement an early-stage prototype and report preliminary results on three balanced test sets of 400 curated web payloads each (SQLi, XSS, SSTI) and a qualitative case study of mitigation generation; an evaluation on IDS- generated alerts and a user study are ongoing and outlined as remaining work.

title: Beyond Single-Turn Privacy: Training-Data Leakage in Conversational RAG
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is known to reduce training-data leakage in single-turn interactions, but whether this protection persists over multi-turn conversations is unclear. We introduce CRELT (Conversational RAG Extraction Leakage Trajectory), a reusable framework that tracks, turn by turn, the real contact details from the training data that a RAG system discloses. CRELT separates retrieval, conversation history, and attack strategy through a full-factorial design, uses a retrieval corpus verified to contain none of the target PII, and counts an item as leaked only when it is absent from the model input at the turn it is produced. In our main experiment, this criterion excludes 29-53% of raw matches that were already present in the input. Across GPT-J-6B, Pythia-6.9B, and Pythia-12B, targeting real Enron contact details, retrieval reduces disclosure under both full and cleared history, consistent with prior single-turn results. A length-matched control with random passages reproduces 91-99.5% of this reduction under cleared history and 47-78% under full history, so much of it comes from the added context rather than from what is retrieved. With retrieval enabled, however, retaining full conversation history increases disclosure by a factor of 3.6-4.9, while retaining only one previous turn already restores disclosure to approximately the full-history level. With retrieval, clearing the history reduces disclosure by 72-79%, but does not eliminate it. These results show that single-turn privacy audits can substantially underestimate training-data leakage in conversational RAG systems and that conversation-history policy is a critical dimension of privacy evaluation.
